newsitem.title: SUDAN: Economists urge Sudan to cut government spending.
newsitem.headline: Economists urge Sudan to cut government spending.

text.p: A state-sponsored economic conference has called on the Sudanese government to stop overspending and press on with economic liberalisation, Khartoum newspapers said on Thursday.
The three-day conference, which brought together more than 1,000 local and international economists, also recommended Sudan quickly end a 13-year-old civil war in the south.
Since 1992, Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir has liberalised the economy by cutting state subsidies and removing controls on the Sudanese pound.

Some economists say Sudan's liberalisation policy is fuelling inflation -- last estimated at 163 percent for the year to the end of July -- but the conference argued the programme had caused abundance rathern than scarcity.
Delegates said the government's policy of continuously borrowing from the central bank to finance ambitious projects like developing railways and petroleum finds was more to blame.

According to the central statistics office, Sudan's money supply has grown to 700 billion pounds this year from 26 billion in 1989, the year the current military government took power in a bloodless coup.
The conference said the war in the south against Christian and animist separatists was also exhausting the country's rapidly dwindling financial resources and particularly much-needed hard currency.
Foreign currency needed to import fuel and vehicles is in short supply due to low export proceeds and falling remittances.
Sudan currently exports goods worth $500 million a year compared to $800 million in the early 1980s.
The delegates recommended Sudan cut business taxes, remove export restrictions, upgrade the quality of its production and encourage traditional enterprises.
They also called on the Khartoum government to improve its relations with traditional donors and trading partners like Egypt and the United States.
The Islamist-dominated military government has managed to alienate most of its neighbours and international partners.

Egypt, Eritrea, Uganda and the United States accuse Khartoum of training militants or rebels seeking to overthrow their governments and the United Nations has slapped limited sanctions on Sudan for failing to extradite three men charged with trying to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in 1995.
Many Arab countries have also expelled Sudanese workers on pretexts ranging from Sudan's pro-Iraqi stand in the 1991 Gulf War to fear of contagion from AIDS.
